messages.subject: [S] Wanted -- Examples of nonlinear statistical models
messages.subject_clean: [S] Wanted -- Examples of nonlinear statistical models
messages.body_plain:
Dear s-news,

   AD Model Builder is a package for creating nonlinear statistical
   models. For the right kind of problem it is very fast. It would be
   a good substitute for C or FORTRAN which users often turn to when
   they wish to solve a computationally intensive nonlinear estimation
   problem. Development with ADMB is much faster and simpler than with
   C or FORTRAN. ADMB can create stand alone programs or routines which
   can be called from Splus (or GAUSS). The best kind of problem to
   test ADMB is a numerically difficult nonlinear problem with a
   lot (say 20-1000) of parameters.

   I am looking for a number of such problems to showcase my software.
   If you think you have such a problem please contact me and we'll
   see if it seems to be a good candidate.

   What you get -- well you get your problem solved and a free copy
   of my software.

   What I get -- I hope you would send a message to this list saying
   how (presumably) happy you are with my software as an extension
   To Splus.

   I am especially interested in comparing the performance of my softwre to
   NUOPT.

   I made this offer to the GAUSS listserver and have completed two
   models for people. Here are their reports to the list.

This is from Mark harris.

Hi Gaussians,

FYI -

We took Dave Fournier up in his offer (see below) to provide code to
perform nonlinear estimation procedures (constrained maximum likelihood)
using his package AD Model Builder for a model we are working on.

This is a description of our experience with his software.

The model is a qualitative response discrete choice model, a combination of
multinomial logit, DOGIT and OGEV models. It is nonlinear maximum
likelihood problem, with typically 50-100 (or more) parameters. We had been
estimating the parameters in GAUSS using CML.
This appeared to take a long time (ie a number of days) and we quite often
had convergence problems (function failing, not appearing to reach "true"
maximums etc.).

The AD Model Builder software was much faster (typically hours as opposed
to days) and generally gave very similar results to CML. Moreover, Dave
transcribed my Gauss code in a matter of days.

We have not yet tried the DLL option of producing a DLL with ADMB which can
be called from GAUSS and so can't comment on that feature. (ADMB also can
produce stand along executables).

We feel that ADMB is potentially a powerful tool to augment GAUSS for this
kind of nonlinear estimation problem, especially when Gauss seems to be
taking a long time to converge.

Cheers

Mark Harris <mark.harris at iaesr.unimelb.edu.au>

****************************************************************************
Mark Harris, Senior Research Fellow
The Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research
University of Melbourne, Vic. 3010, Australia
tel +61 3 9344 5354: fax +61 3 9344 5630
****************************************************************************

And this is a report from Gary King.

Dave Fournier <otter at otter-rsch.com> has a product call ADbuilder, which
maximizes functions (among other things) using automatic derivatives.
(Automatic derivatives are analytically computed derivatives done
automatically:  the user only needs to enter the objective function, as in
the equivalent of the loglik() proc in Gauss' MAXLIK.)  Dave, Ken Benoit,
and I worked to get a few of my examples into his program (he did the
coding) as a test run.  The deal was that we'd report on whatever we
found.

ADbuilder is a product separate from Gauss, but we were able to pull his
compiled code in via the foreign language interface.  The results were
really impressive.  The speed was between 13 and 68 times faster than
Gauss' maxlik without analytical derivatives specified. Obviously, adding
analytical derivatives would make maxlik faster, but that would have been
extremely tedious in the examples we gave him (and I'd rather spend
computer time than human time of course).

Ken and I now plan to learn how to use his program ourselves.

messages.subject: [S] "patch-to-patch" for first S-PLUS 2000 Release 2 update available
messages.subject_clean: [S] "patch-to-patch" for first S-PLUS 2000 Release 2 update available
messages.body_plain:
By popular request, for those who installed the FIRST release of the S-PLUS
2000 patch ONLY, a patch-to-the-patch is available which upgrades those
users to the second release of the patch.  This small patch (550Kb) is
available from:

http://www.mathsoft.com/splus/resources/download/splus2000r2PATCH.htm

Some (hopefully anticipatory) questions and answers:

1. How can I tell if I need this patch-to-the-patch?

A. You only need this patch if you downloaded and installed the FIRST
release of the S-PLUS 2000 Release 2 patch, which briefly appeared on the
MathSoft website on November 1 until it was withdrawn on November 3.  To
check whether you need this patch, start S-PLUS 2000 and choose "About
S-PLUS" from the Help Menu.
        * If "Rev Date" is 26 Oct 1999, you need this patch
        * If "Rev Date" is 5 Nov 1999, you already have the latest release
of S-PLUS 2000
        * If the version is identified as "S-PLUS 2000 Professional Release
1" or "S-PLUS 2000 Professional Release 1a", you should download the full
patch from www.mathsoft.com/splus to upgrade to Release 2.

2. Is there any difference between S-PLUS upgraded with this
patch-to-the-patch, and S-PLUS upgraded with the rereleased patch?

A. No.  Both versions of S-PLUS are identical in every way.

3. I successfully patched S-PLUS R1 or R1a with the previous version of this
patch.  What changes to S-PLUS does this patch-to-the-patch make?

A. This version corrects four specific problems found in the previous
version of the patch:

  a. the original patch did not detect the edition, so that it could
silently patch (incorrectly) editions of S-PLUS 2000 other than the
stand-alone version of S-PLUS 2000 Professional.

  b. a problem in 3D Trellis graphics using multiple pages which caused a
General Protection Fault (GPF) has been corrected.

  c. clearing or deleting row(s) in the Data window resulted in only the
first cell in the row being changed to NA, rather than the whole row, or the
row NOT being removed when the Delete key was pressed.

  d. the Commands window, as in Release 1, does not close when you change
Workspaces.

4.  Since both patches are officially labeled "Release 2", how will the next
patch (i.e. Release 3) be affected by having two different Release 2's in
circulation? 

A. Any Release 3 will be able to patch both "Release 2"s with a single
patch.

5. As an only occasional user of S+, when the smoke settles could you put a
single patch on your web page which incorporates the patch, the patch to the
patch, and whatever else is to be included ... in a single download? 

A. The patch made available November 10 incorporates the original patch plus
the four changes described under question 1. If you still have R1 or R1a,
that is the only download you need. The "patch to the patch" is ONLY for
users who successfully patched their R1 or R1a installations with the
original patch.

messages.subject: [S] Re: Recoding Data by Vectorization
messages.body_plain:
I would like to thank Bill Venables, Don McKenzie, George Tomlinson, Nick
Ellis, John Bjornar Bremnes for their responses to my question. I included
the original question and the responses below. Since my original question
was stated as "improving efficiency", two of the responses emphasized
slightly different aspects of computation than what I had in mind.  I have
not had a chance to try the suggested solutions yet. I decided to summarize
them without much delay.  Again, thank you. 

Original Question:
======================================
Given a matrix, say z, as follows, it is desired to replace the 0's with
the column means. The 9's are going to be regarded as missing and therefore
set to NA. (Both 0 and 9 need to be excluded from the computation of the
column means.)

  V1 V2 
1  4  5
2  0  9
3  9  0
4  4  5

# copy z to t and compute column means by ignoring 0 and 9 
t <- z
t [t == 0 | t == 9] <- NA
mn <- apply(t, 2, mean, na.rm=T)
# replace 0's with column means
i.mat <- matrix(as.numeric(z==0), nrow=nrow(z), ncol=ncol(z))
mn.val <- i.mat %*% diag(mn)
j.mat <- matrix(as.numeric(z!=0), nrow=nrow(z), ncol=ncol(z))
z.rep <- z * j.mat + mn.val
# set 9's to NA and print result
z.rep [z.rep == 9] <- NA
z.rep

Although the above does the job, those who are more experienced with the
vectorization capabilities of S-Plus may accomplish the same in a more
efficient way. I'll post the improvements that the experienced users
suggest. Thank you.  
============================================

Bill Venables wrote: 

Is it the case that (a) the 9's are regarded as missing but not replaced
and (b) the 0's are also regarded as missing, but replaced by the mean of
all the others?

If so (your verbal description was not too clear) I think I would go for a
solution that made what you were doing much more obvious.  I don't think
this will save you much time, but it will make it easy to follow.

> fixit <- function(x) {
          z <- x == 0
          x[z | x == 9] <- NA
          x[z] <- mean(x, na.rm = T)
          x
}

t.fixed <- apply(t, 2, fixit)

This replaces most of your post processing with a single call to apply(),
which you have to do anyway.

===========================================
Don McKenzie wrote:

You can actually use the matrix algebra in S more efficiently for column
means than apply(), which is more general, does.  Here is one example,
which is probably not optimal, but gives the idea:

mat.cmeans <-
function(mat)
#calculate a vector of column means of a matrix
{
        len <- length(mat[, 1])
        (t(mat) %*% rep(1, len))/len
}
==================================================
George Tomlinson suggested:

There's probably some way to do this without
"for", but this works:

z <- matrix(c(4,0,9,4,5,9,0,5),ncol=2)
z[z==9] <- NA
for(i in 1:2){
zeroes <- z[,i]==0
z[zeroes,i] <- mean(z[!zeroes,i],na.rm=T)
}
z
==================================================

Nick Ellis wrote:

Use matrix subscripting:

> dat <- as.matrix(read.table(file = "clipboard"))
> dat
  V1 V2 
1  4  5
2  0  9
3  9  0
4  4  5
> Rows <- row(dat)[dat == 0]
> Cols <- col(dat)[dat == 0] # do these before we set some NAs
> dat[dat == 9] <- NA
> mn <- apply(dat, 2, mean, na.rm = T)
> dat[cbind(Rows, Cols)] <- mn[Cols] # dat has to be a matrix - won't work
on data frame
> dat
    V1   V2 
1 4.00 5.00
2 2.67   NA
3   NA 3.33
4 4.00 5.00

====================================
John Bjornar Bremnes suggested:

Maybe something like
m <- apply( z, 2, mean, na.rm=T )
z <- sapply( 1:ncol(z), function(k){ z[z[,k]==0,k] <- m[k] } )
z[z==9] <- NA

I have not tried this, but hope this helps. 

========================================================

End of responses

=====================================================
Dr. K. Buyukkurt, Associate Professor
Marketing Department, Faculty of Commerce and Administration
Concordia University, 1450 De Maisonneuve Blvd West
Montreal, Quebec H3G 1M8, Canada

messages.subject: [S] Memory usage.
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users,

last Thursday, nov. 11th, around 14h.30 I launched the following S+ job.  When I
left at 16h.30 it was still running, since I was off on Friday I thought there
was plenty of time for the job to finish untill Monday morning!  But surprise,
it was still running at 8h30 this morning.   Needless to say that I canceled it
but I would like to understand what happened?  I know that S+ is not the
greatest at handling large data sets and at managing memory usage but over 84
hours on a Pentium 350 Mhz. machine with 256M of RAM and 1G of swapfile running
on NT 4.0 is a lot of CPU time!  When I came in my collegues said: "This the
stat. package you want us to buy more licenses for?  No thank you, we'll stay
with SAS."  Can I blame them?

Here are the specs. on my input data set:

> dim(vol05.all)
[1] 179764     25

> vol05.sumvars
[1] "unsous"   "unsousf"  "nsinvolt" "en15volt" "en15vold"

> vol05.groupvars
 [1] "ageass"   "assu3an"  "mtass"    "nblogis"  "fum"      "rprof"
 [7] "vol"      "nbsin3an" "const"    "creanc"   "dcontra"  "nbancomp"
[13] "pourcass" "protect"

The variables in "sumvars" are continuous variables and the variables in
"groupvars" have anywhere from 2 to 12 levels.  Here is the
call to the culpright function and the function itself, any insights would be
most welcomed.

vol05.dfsummary <- dfsummary(vol05.all, vol05.sumvars, vol05.groupvars)

function (dat, sumvars, groupvars)
{
# Date    : March 1999
# Purpose : Will call "menuDescribe" getting summaries for variables "sumvars"
#           and grouping by "groupvars", the data is in the data frame "dat".
# Parameters : dat      : input data frame.
#              sumvars  : variables for which summaries will be obtained.
#              groupvars: grouping variables.

ttt <- menuDescribe(data = dat, variables = sumvars,
                 grouping.variables = groupvars,
                 max.numeric.levels=10, nbins=6, min.p=T, first.quant.p=F,
                 mean.p=T, median.p=F, third.quant.p=F, max.p=T, nobs.p=T,
                 valid.n.p=F, var.p=F, stdev.p=T, sum.p=T, factors.too.p=T,
                 print.p=F)
ttt
}

Hello to everyone,

thanks to Ed Callahan, Bert Gunter and David Smith (from Mathsoft) for their
quick replies.  David Smith supplied the following remarks, and he is right I
didn't neither needed nor wanted summaries for all possible combinations of the
categorical variables but summaries for each level of the categorical variable
separately!    When I saw his solution it rang bells and, shame on me , digging
in my notes for old project I found that I took the same approach, as his
suggestion, a while back!  The original message and David's solution follow for
the ones still interested!

Thanks to all responders,

Gérald Jean

télephone            : (418) 835-8839
télecopieur          : (418) 835-5865

"In God we trust all others must bring data"

---------------

> ttt <- menuDescribe(data = dat, variables = sumvars,
>                  grouping.variables = groupvars,
>                  max.numeric.levels=10, nbins=6, min.p=T, first.quant.p=F,
>                  mean.p=T, median.p=F, third.quant.p=F, max.p=T, nobs.p=T,
>                  valid.n.p=F, var.p=F, stdev.p=T, sum.p=T,
factors.too.p=T,
>                  print.p=F)

The grouping.variables argument will provide summaries for a number of
subsets of the data.  There will be as many subsets as there are
*combinations* of the levels of the variables specified by this argument.
For your data this means anywhere between 2^14=16384 and 12^14 = 1.3 million
trillion subsets.  That's a lot of output to digest -- is this really what
you intended?

Maybe

for(v in vol05.groupvars)
     menuDescribe(vol05.all, variables=sumvars, grouping.variables=v)

is more like what you were after.

Sincerely,

{

Solution:
=======

 After a bit, too much, of fooling around I found the culpright.  The x-axis
labels were factor levels and I noticed that for all the off position labels the
character "|" was part of the label generated from the factor level.  I was
using the "|" in some of the factor levels for a short of "or" (for exemple:
"this or that" was coded as "this | that").  I suppose that the "|" is used as
some carriage control character or tab or something?  As soon as I changed the
factor levels where the "|" was appearing all was fine.

messages.subject: Re: [S] cox ph with bootstrap function
messages.body_plain:
The message comes up in two situations

        1. One of the coefficients is essentially infinite.  Bootstrap
percentile confidence intervals will not be bothered by this, but an estimate of
se might be useless.

   2. With hightly skewed or correlated covariates, the warning can be issued 
inappropriately.   
   
  Infinite coefficients occur in the Cox model whenever the covariates
can define a subset with no events.  The hazard ratio with respect to this
subset is x/0 for some positive number x, which is infinite.  I don't view
this as a failure of the model, just as a subset with perfect prediction.
(The approximation behind the Wald test,  beta/se(beta), fall apart in this
instance however and it becomes useless.  Use the likelihood ratio).

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: [S] Aberrant behaviour with BIBs
messages.body_plain:
These comments refer to Splus 5.1 on Unix.

The fine print of the documentation warns that 'model.tables' does not work
correctly with unbalanced data, but it produces output nevertheless. With a
BIB design the output is correct if the treatment factor contrasts are
orthogonal, otherwise not. Since the form of the contrasts is hidden, and
since a user might be forgiven for thinking that a BIB design generates
balanced data, I consider Splus's behaviour a little immoral.  If only
means are wanted, the contrast coding should be irrelevant.

The problem arises in 'eff.aovlist' which gives the anwers I would expect
only for orthogonal contrasts.

Example from Statistical Design and Analysis of Experiments, P W M John.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: counting radio stations
messages.body_plain:
S.D. Byers and Julian Taylor provided simple tests
for 6000 observations of the form

     N<- 6000
     revenue <- rnorm(N,mean=100, sd=10)
     market <- factor(sample(1:70, replace=T, size=N))
     owner <- factor(sample(1:100, replace=T, size=N))

     fred <- tapply(revenue, list(market,owner), sum)

which works nicely.  However, I have 270 markets
and 1932 owners in 6055 observations.  When the
above code is amended to reflect these numbers,

     N<- 6055
     revenue <- rnorm(N,mean=100, sd=10)
     market <- factor(sample(1:270, replace=T, size=N))
     owner <- factor(sample(1:1932, replace=T, size=N))

     fred <- tapply(revenue, list(market,owner), sum)

then S-PLUS 2000 (now release 2) on a 300MHz PII
with 48M Ram and 100M free on the harddrive
hangs after filling up the disk space, which is what
I get with my real data.

The upshot seems to be that while tapply will do
the job for 70 markets and 100 owners, it won't
do the job for 270 markets and 1932 owners.

What I wound up doing is looping over the markets
and, for each market, using tapply on revenue and
owner, and then using cat to write the market results
to a file.

Thanks to all,

Bruce

messages.body_plain:
Are you really interested in a huge matrix, most of whose cells are empty?
Better would be a 3-column table with heading market, owner and sum. Here's
how.

Create a new factor whose levels are all the existing combinations of market
and owner.

market.owner <- interaction(market,owner,drop=T)

Then do tapply on this new factor

fred <- tapply(revenue, list(market.owner), sum)

You can then bind the results together using the undocumented unpaste().

Here's the idea in action
N <- 10
revenue <- rnorm(N,mean=100, sd=10)
market <- factor(sample(1:270, replace=T, size=N))
owner <- factor(sample(1:1932, replace=T, size=N))
market.owner <- interaction(market,owner,drop=T)
fred <- tapply(revenue, list(market.owner), sum)
df <- as.data.frame(c(unpaste(market.owner,sep="."),list(fred)))
names(df) <- c("market","owner","sum")
df
         market owner   sum

187.1251    187  1251  96.6
  40.639     40   639  99.6

That last example wouldn't work in general. I should have said
levels(market.owner). Here's the corrected form.

N <- 10
revenue <- rnorm(N,mean=100, sd=10)
market <- factor(sample(1:270, replace=T, size=N))
owner <- factor(sample(1:1932, replace=T, size=N))
market.owner <- interaction(market,owner,drop=T)
fred <- tapply(revenue, list(market.owner), sum)
df <- as.data.frame(c(unpaste(levels(market.owner),sep="."),list(fred)))
names(df) <- c("market","owner","sum")
df

messages.subject: [S]: need help with .C interface
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm attempting to familiarize myself with the .C interface.   I have
written a simple C function shown below along with the S script that calls
it.  It's been a long time since I have programmed in C as well as using
the .C interface so I welcome any suggestions.  

---------------------------------------------
#C code

#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

 void test_mean(double *par, int *tyme, int n_tyme, int bdgrp, int agegrp,
double *means)
 {
   int i;
   for (i=0; i<n_tyme; ++i) {
       
        means[i] = par[0] + par[1]*bdgrp + par[2]*agegrp + 
                  (par[3] + par[4]*bdgrp) * exp(- par[5]*tyme[i]);
   }
 }

---------------------------------------------
#S code

"testmean" = 

#test .C interface by calculating exp mean model.

function(){
  
  beta = c(0.260, 0.441, 0.071, 0.523, 0.015, 0.012)
  means = vector(mode = "double", length = length(tyme))
  tyme = c(2, 14, 25, 40, 55, 81,107)

  cat("\nMean:  ", means, "\n")

  tmp = .C("test_mean", beta, tyme, length(tyme), 1, 0,  means,
     CLASSES=c("numeric", "numeric", "integer", "integer", "integer",
               "numeric"))

  cat("\nMean:  ", means, "\n\n")
  cat("\ntmp:  ", tmp[[6]], "\n")  

}

---------------------------------------------
I ran make and had no apparent trouble.

Splus make
cc -I${SHOME}/include  -Xa    -c  testmean.c
/opt/local/splus5.1/cmd/Splus5 LIBRARY S.so  testmean.o

---------------------------------------------
I run into trouble when I call the S function:

testmean()

Mean:   0 0 0 0 0 0 0
Terminating S Session: Signal: bad address signal

---------------------------------------------

A rather cryptic ending.  I'm not sure if the problem is with matching
argument classes, in my S code or C code.  Any suggestions or pointers (no
pun intended) are greatly appreciated.  

Please e-mail me and I'll summarize to the list.

messages.body_plain:
Mixed-effects modelling is the best approach, however, the current version
of nlme (3.0) does not fit models to ordinal responses. I would recommend
the NONMEM package which is most often used in pharmacokinetic and
pharmacodynamic area, but is quite universal and is able also to cope with
binary responses, counts, survivals, etc. The URL is
http://c255.ucsf.edu/nonmem0.html

messages.subject: [S] let makes things better
messages.body_plain:
Is a slogan of a worldwide wellknown Dutch electronic company (Philips),
however not always succesful in doing so.
Anyway, although I am not a 'button' fan one of the nice things of Splus
4.0 and higher is the way you generate reports quite easily by a click
of the mouse. There are however a few nuissances:

1. Splus-2000 no longer supports the RTF-format, that is a pity, why
should every company have is own 'standard' (in this case .srp). This is
NOT an improvement.
2. When analysing data I hate to switch in the options menu between  the
output routings: Default, Commands, report. A much, much better way
would be to have a BUTTON in EACH report-, command- or default-window,
where you select your  output routing (on/off with a nice red and green
light) while simultaneously allowing you to have more then one output
channel open! The latter is especially nice if you just concentrate on
the analysis and you don't want to switch beteen script -report or
command-report.

Are there any supporters for this improvement, (or must i say change)?
siem heisterkamp

messages.subject: [S] better counting idea?
messages.body_plain:
I'm thinking there is a more efficient way to do some counting,
essentially modified freq counting.
I'm open to any kind of suggestions! Hopefully my comments explain the
process.

Much thanks in advance.
________________________________________
freq_rep(0,3) #makes three values (now zero) for frequency from smallest
(1) to largest (3)
rat_rep(0,6) #makes 6 values (now zero) for rat (ratio)
#count from the bottom unique freqs til sum(brax)/3 is exceeded then
back 1#
for(i in 1:length(brax))    #returns an integer of the length of brax
{
  if(freq[1] < sum(brax)/3) #when brax sum is greater than a third of
brax
  {
    freq[1]_freq[1]+brax[i] #get that number and put in the first freq
value
  }
  else {
    j_i
    break
  }
}
for(k in j:length(brax)) {
  if(freq[2] < sum(brax)/3) {
    freq[2]_freq[2]+brax[k]
  }
  else {
    l_k
    break
  }
}
freq[3]_sum(brax[l:length(brax)])
rat[1]_j-1
rat[2]_l-j
rat[3]_length(brax)-l+1
rat[4]_length(brax)
rat[5]_sum(brax)
n_rat[2]/rat[3]
nsq_n*n

I have tried to do the second half with guiModify, but I haven't been able to

messages.subject_clean: [S] Bug? Splus PostScript driver with image plots
messages.body_plain:
Image plots with irregular grids do not appear correctly in PostScript
files. Try this:

 Create a matrix with an irregular spacing:

 x_c(1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512)
 y_x
 z_matrix(1:100,10,10)

 image it on an X device:

 image(x,y,z)

 looks fine - the grid squares are larger as x and y increase.

 now make a PostScript file copy:

 dev.print(file="nonreg.ps")

 Printing or viewing the resulting PS file shows the matrix
 as a _regular_ grid, even though the axes are labelled right.

 Looking at the PostScript output it seems to totally ignore the
irregular X and Y spacing. It just scales a pixmap to the plot
area.

 This happens with Splus 3.4 and Splus 5.1 on Solaris and Linux. Has
anyone else noticed this before?

 I've emailed the Splus bug address (bugs at statsci.com) but no feedback
yet...

Barry Rowlingson

Computing Officer/Research Associate
Maths and Stats

messages.body_plain:
I wrote a function with an argument (called data) that can be a vector or a
data.frame.  If the input is a data.frame, the calucations are done for each
column.  There is another argument (called resp.label) used for labeling the
results which defaults to the names of the data.frame columns.

The function starts with this bit of code:
   if(is.vector(data)){
     data <- as.data.frame(data)
     names(data) <- deparse(substitute(data))
     invisible(resp.label)
   }

If the invisible() comand isn't included then resp.label doesn't work correctly
when invoked latter.  I suspect this has something to do with lazy evaluation,
but I don't really understand the mechanics and would appreciate any insight.
And of course I'm open to learn of better ways.

I'll summarize to the list.
Thanks, KJJ

messages.subject: RE: [S] "Repeated" Ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
I have been using WinBUGS for estimating models for serial ordinal
data, by fitting autoregrssive setups for the latent variable
typically posited to underlie ordinal data: e.g.,

y_t^* = X_t \beta + \rho y_{t-1}^* + \epsilon_t, 
\rho \in (-1, 1), \epsilon_t ~ N(0,\sigma^2) \forall t
y_t = 0 <=> y_t^* < 0
y_t = 1 <=> 0 < y_t^* < \lambda_1
y_t = 2 <=> \lambda_1 < y_t^* < \lambda_2
...
y_t = J <=> \lambda_{J-1} < y_t^*  

this could be easily generalized to panel data/repeated measures.  See
http://tamarama.stanford.edu/mcmc/delegation.pdf for an example and code

-- simon jackman

messages.subject: Re: [S] data visualization references
messages.body_plain:
Visualization has nothing to do with "modernity". In my student days in math
courses in engineering school before WWII, "visualization" referred to creating
and examining data graphics. We were expected, where possible, to present a
graphic with each problem answer on our exams.

My framework for teaching statistics became: 1. y=f(x) is simply a shorthand
statement of how to construct a graphic, or in modern terms it is an imaging
language statement and 2. in applied statistics if you cannot see an effect
with graphics you will never see it with statistics; a statistical test or
estimate simply asks whether to attribute what one sees to chance. There are
some incredibly stupid research reports in the scientific literature which
would never have seen the light of day or would have been interpreted far
differently had someone first created an image of the data rather than just
manipulating a number set.

What is modern is that we now have marvelous devices which will create the
visuals for us in far more useful forms.

> > paper uses a "visualization" technique to analyze the data". I have, of
> > course, referred to Cleveland's book, but the referee is not satisfied. I
> > have only very little space to work with, can any one point me to an
> > independent reference for the current status of visualization in modern
> > data analysis and statistics? Any suggestions for a brief definition of
> > "data visualization"? 
> 
> I just met the same problem and I made a private reply to Willem.
> 
> It looks like some (many ?) referees don't like the style of Trellis

> statistical "modernity" and "editorial advisory boards" ? I feel that
> Trellis display is much more than fancy and glitters and should be
> defended. I would be interested if someone could propose some general
> guidelines to avoid this kind of problem.

On Fri, 19 Nov 1999 gordon.harrington at uni.edu wrote:

> Visualization has nothing to do with "modernity". In my student days in math
> courses in engineering school before WWII, "visualization" referred to 
> creating
> and examining data graphics. We were expected, where possible, to present a
> graphic with each problem answer on our exams.
> 
> My framework for teaching statistics became: 1. y=f(x) is simply a shorthand
> statement of how to construct a graphic, or in modern terms it is an imaging
> language statement and 2. in applied statistics if you cannot see an effect
> with graphics you will never see it with statistics; a statistical test or
> estimate simply asks whether to attribute what one sees to chance. There are
> some incredibly stupid research reports in the scientific literature which
> would never have seen the light of day or would have been interpreted far
> differently had someone first created an image of the data rather than just
> manipulating a number set.

Sure, but not quite always. One of my favourite demos at the moment is a
functional MRI dataset of 2 million points (100 sets of images in sequence)
in which no one can see anything unless it is pointed out to them (and then
only a very few can) yet I can get significance levels less than 10^{-4}
from a statistical test of there being something there (and there is).  It
is the ability to do problems that are beyond the human visual system that
are `modern' (and as you pointed out, depend on hardware developments).  
As I understand it `data visualization' is a _much_ larger research subject
than Cleveland's (1993) book (and was in 1993). Things like projection
pursult, multidimensional scaling, correspondence analysis, biplots, ...
are important data visualization tools (and dare I say much more important
than Trellis(TM) graphics), and there is a computer science literature,
even on `caves' and virtual reality immersion, ....

Brian Ripley

messages.subject: [S] Spatial statistics
messages.body_plain:
I will soon be doing some research on discrete spatial data. In
particular, I'm looking at output from algorithms that operate on Doppler
weather-radar data.  These algorithms try to detect certain features known
to be dynamically or kinematically associated with severe weather,
providing us with point locations every 5 or 6 min of where these things
might be. We are very interested in knowing if these locations are
distributed uniformly in space and time, and if they are not, where and
when there are significant concentrations and voids.

        I suspect that the S-Plus spatial stats add-on package would be
useful in helping approach this problem, but I know little about rigorous
spatial statistics.  I suspect there is expertise in the group on this
but, more to the point, would the Spatial Stats package be a useful tool,
or would I do better to try something different?  If the latter, I'm open
to suggestions.  Also, I'm open to introductory references on this general
topic, though I don't particularly want spatial statistics to become my
life's work :)  I'm happy to take this to private e-mail to save the group
from what might become a rather specialized discussion only perfially
related to S-Plus.  Thanks!

                Kim Elmore, [N5OP, PP ASMEL/Glider 2232456]

marginal frequencies.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Ploting Data with Symbols Marked as Counts
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Ploting Data with Symbols Marked as Counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi, all,

Here I would like to express my sincere thanks and appreciation to Bill
Dunlap, Prof. Frank Harrell, and Eric Lecoutre for their quick reponse and 
truely help! 

Minutes ago, I posted the following questions

> I'm in the following situation. With data, say,
>       x <- sample(1:10, 100,replace=T)
>       y <- sample(10:20, 100, replace=T)
> I want to plot y vs. x. Obviously, considerable points would overlap each
> other. So I'd like to mark each point as its frequency count, rather than
> a single dot. In SAS, this could be achievable by defining a new
> variable 'count' and whence using PROC PLOT; PLOT x*y = count;  
> > I don't know if there exists any easier way in Splus to do this without
> running into too many loops.  Please advise.
> Also, to count the frequncy, the following way would be very helpful.
>      aggregate(rep(1, length(x)), list(x,y), sum)

Bill's Solution:
=====================

       Count <- aggregate(rep(1, length(x)), list(x,y), sum)
       names(Count)<-c("x","y","count")
       Count$x<-as.numeric(as.character(Count$x))
       Count$y<-as.numeric(as.character(Count$y))
       xyplot(y~x, panel=function(x,y,subscripts, groups)text(x,y,
            lab=groups[subscripts]), groups=count, data=Count)

Which does the perfect job!

Also, Prof. Harrell suggested the following:
===============================================

symbol.freq in the Hmisc library will do perhaps a better job than SAS.It
will compute frequencies of all x-y combinations and draw symbols at the
x-y coordinates (circles or thermometers) whose size is proportional to
the frequency. For your case, try symbol.freq(x, y, 'circle').
symbol.freq can also show marginal frequencies.

Best Regards to all,
Xiaogang

> > Date: Fri, 19 Nov 1999 12:00:14 -0500 (EST)
> > From: "J. S. Gangolly" <gangolly at csc.albany.edu>
> > 
> > 
> > It is sad that we should be spending so much of our time
> > worrying about problems that really are from Bill Gates
> > arena. I have held steadfast to my old-fashioned
> > TeX/LaTeX guns till now, but am not sure how long I can
> > endure. It is a shame that even many computing oriented
> > conferences/journals/funding agencies should be
> > insisting on Bill Gates formats, when productivity
> > could be enhanced with what is freely available and
> > well-respected.
> 
> > Jagdish S. Gangolly, Associate Professor (j.gangolly at albany.edu)
> 
> Think *you're* old fashoned?  I still use troff, and with pleasure 8^)
> 
> It seems to me that there are several legal/ethical issues involved
> here.  It seems outrageous that *any* organization dealing with agents
> outside of itself should mandate the use of a particular single-vendor
> commercial product such as Word.  Support for *open standards* that
> allow multiple players seems critically important to continued
> innovation and collaboration in the computing realm.  It may be that
> one day we will arrive at the point that our various favored document
> preparation systems will have filters to translate into an open
> standards-based lingua franca, say XML.
> Until that day comes, we have to show individual and collective spine
> and "just say no."  Organizations that insist on using single products
> need to be brought up short for dissing open standards (to say nothing
> of caving in to apparent monopolies).

This is a side issue but a critically important one, in my view.  I agree 
entirely with the two speakers above (though I would never use troff, Ugh!  :-)

One of the biggest shocks for me in passing from the relative freedom of the
University environment to the narrower public sector research environment was
to see the degree to which this insidious standardization on the (at best)
mediocre has already taken place.  It is simply assumed that you will be using
a Windows machine, Word, Excel, Access, Power Point, Outlook and the whole
hideous mess.  No one thinks twice about sending a huge email with an
"attachment" in Word or Excel to an entire workforce and *assuming* that you
can not only read it, but you can modify it and send the damn thing back!
(There will even be people reading this wondering what the hell I am talking
about, I'm sure.  One of the secretaries here just looks at me incredulously
every time this comes up.  "What do you mean, Bill, when you say you don't have
a PC *or* a Mac, but you have a `real computer'?  What else *is* there?")

I was recently asked to write a short article on graphics for (here's a fine
irony coming up) a "Quality" Magazine.  It was only by fluke that I discovered
that they were simply presuming I would send them camera ready copy in *Word*.
Of course I refused.  Eventually, though, we compromised on pdf.  This dodge
may offer a partial way round this huge Microsoft roadblock, but only for
typesetting of course.  PDF doesn't have the open source transparency of TeX/
LaTeX, but pdflatex works very well, as does epstopdf for graphical inserts.

It is not at all hard to write a document that compiles into postscript using
latex+dvips or into pdf using pdflatex without changing the text at all.  It
does require duplicate copies of graphical inserts to be available, though, the
eps file and the .pdf equivalent.  (I am indebted to Berwin Turlach for
showing me this neat trick, by the way.)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: [S] multivariable paired t-test.
messages.body_plain:
John Sorkin asks:

> 
> We are all familiar with the unpaired t-test, and its multivariable form,
> ANOVA.  We are also familiar with the paired t-test. Is there a multivariable
> form of the paired t-test? 

I would express it by saying that the unpaired t-test is the simplest case of a
single classification ANOVA.  In this sense a paired t-test is the simplest
case of a double classification ANOVA (with one observation per cell, the
so-called `randomized block design').

> Perhaps lme with the correct covariance structure
> would be my solution, but I do not know what covariance structure to use.

Much simpler, I'd say.  The paired t-test only tests the treatment effect
(which we would usually think of as a fixed effect) and in this case the
computation is the same whether we think of the sampling units as constituting
a fixed or a random effect.  So all you need is aov().  

If you wanted to estimate variance components you might use varcomp() or lme()
but this again would be using a sledgehammer to crack a peanut...  The usual
covariance structure within a block (or sampling unit) in this case is
"compound symmetry", a fancy way of saying "equal variances and equal
covariances".

Bill Venables.
--

accomplished by using Hotelling's T^2, i.e. MANOVA. I would like to thank

greatly appreciate that even "basic" questions are answered by the members of
this listserv group.

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

I'm trying to build a DLL file to load in Splus2000/Win98. My C code
has some printf() calls, so, as indicated in the Programmer's Guide, I
included "S.h" and "newredef.h" and managed the code to compile without
warnings (I'm using gcc/2.95/mingw32). My problems started when I tried
to build the .dll file. Specifically, I can't link some S objects (like
S_newio_printf). 

I've checked the S-news archives and found a similar question posted by
Steve Buyske last August. Following Prof. B. Ripley's reply to that
e-mail I tried to build my own "Spqe" library (assuming that the
objects I need are indeed in Sqpe.dll). I quote Prof. Ripley's message:

> You need to make it, by
>
> dlltool --dllname Sqpe.dll Sqpe.def --output-lib libSqpe.a         
>
> where Sqpe.def sits in the SHOME/lib directory (and needs the 
> development libraries installed), and I had to remove a couple 
> of $****. entries from Sqpe.def to get this to work.

To my surprise, I can't seem to find "Sqpe.def" anywhere in my hard
drive. 

My question are: (a) is there a Sqpe.def file in the Win98 distribution
of Splus2000 and I did not install it?; (b) if not, is there a way of
creating Sqpe.def from Sqpe.dll?; (c) if not, is there any other way to
link with objects in Sqpe.dll? 

(I hope I'm not overlooking some simple detail here....)

I'll summarize the answers I receive to the list in the next couple of
days. 

Matias Salibian

University of British Columbia

> specifications.  
> (The version I have is S-PLUS for Windows version 3.3

Well, that is part of library MASS, and you don't seem to want to give the
author any credit for his work!  The exact algorithms are in the S code,
and the background theory in

B. D. Ripley (1996) Pattern Recognition and Neural Networks. CUP,

especially Chapter 3, and more description of how to use it is in MASS
(the book).

As a general point, a great deal of the detail of S can be found by reading
the code.

messages.subject: Re: [S] data visualization references
messages.body_plain:
About scientific visualization and Edward Tufte.

A person at NASA-Ames, Al Globus, has written up some words following the
guidelines of Edward Tufte, in a humorous and satirical way.

(If any of you have ever seen the "Viz-O-matic" video about scientific
visualization shown at SIGGRAPH some years ago, then you know what I
mean.)

"14 Ways to Say Nothing with Scientific Visualization," A. Globus,
E. Raible, IEEE Computer, July 1994.

Which you can get in postscript form. 

http://www.nas.nasa.gov/Pubs/TechReports/RNRreports/aglobus/RNR-92-006/RNR-92-006.html

The abstract follows. Hope this brightens your snowy Monday. 

"Scientific visualization can be used to produce very beautiful
images.  Frequently users and others not properly initiated into the
mysteries of visualization research fail to appreciate the artistic
qualities of these images. Scientists will frequently use our work to
needlessly understand the data from which it is derived. This paper
describes a a number of effective techniques to confound such
pernicious activity."

Amara

P.S. I attended an all-day seminar from Tufte some years ago, and I
never looked at data and information in the same way afterwards. Tufte
is really great.

--

messages.subject: [S] RTF/ facilitating direction of output stream
messages.subject_clean: [S] RTF/ facilitating direction of output stream
messages.body_plain:
Last week i  put a question on the list with regard to some irritating
'improvements' in S-Plus 2000, and asked some comment / or support on
it.
My original intro was:

1. Splus-2000 no longer supports the RTF-format, that is a pity, why
should every company have is own 'standard' (in this case .srp). This is
NOT an improvement.
2. When analysing data I hate to switch in the options menu between  the
output routings: Default, Commands, report. A much, much better way
would be to have a BUTTON in EACH report-, command- or default-window,
where you select your  output routing (on/off with a nice red and green
light) while simultaneously allowing you to have more then one output
channel open! The latter is especially nice if you just concentrate on
the analysis and you don't want to switch beteen script -report or
command-report.

the question; support etc:

I found support by several  contributors of the s-news list, among
others:
Frank E Harrell Jr [fharrell at virginia.edu]
Michael Prager [Mike.Prager at noaa.gov]
and several dutch contributors (of our dutch list s-nieuws)
Michael Prager pointed out that aparantly Mathsoft already has the
intention to change the RTF format back.
Anyway this question provoked another line in the debate:
Wintle-tools or something else.
>>From Longhow Lam [lam at candiensten.nl] I heard that MathSoft has ideas to
integrate S-plus further with word and excell.
Personally I don't like that idea at all!. 
Please make S-PLus not more dependent on Microsoft. There are many
statisticians who use both windows and unix/linux, e.g. sometimes you
develop a program on the PC, but it must run on a unix sytem for
'production'.  *.PDF is an option which can be read by both unix and
wintel systems and even apple.
Renaud Lancelot [lancelot at telecomplus.sn] has written a bundle of
functions which enable users to publish their data in HTML-format. 

So Mathsoft, 
We have again WEB-democracy (the "wall" has fallen, but what does that
mean, it just has shifted westwards) : it looks that there is a 100%
YES-vote (no No-votes anyway) for the improvements and some concerns
about the wintel dictatorship.
Siem Heisterkamp

messages.subject: [S] A contrarian's view re: MS
messages.body_plain:
Hi all:

A contrarian's view just to spice up the discussion.

IMPORTANT DISCLAIMERS. These views are my own and in no way reflect any
opinions of my employer or my colleagues. Also, I'm no special fan of nor
have any financial interest in MS (though I wish I did ... sigh!).

Although I know this may irritate all you free thinkers, I believe that
there are good arguments and data to support the notions that:

1. Standardization (software AND hardware) brings an enormous savings in
efficiency and support costs.Try running and SUPPORTING -- something
academic types generally do for themselves, but not so in business - a large
information infrastructure otherwise. We do not have the luxury of big
computer science departments nor cheap student labor, I might add.

2. Standardization of anything inherently brings the cost of mediocrity.
That is the nature of giving up optimized solutions. For academe, this
tradeoff may well be inappropriate, but in most business environments, it is
essential.

3. So the issue is to standardize on what. Here I rejoin the crowd. MS has
used blatant and rapacious business practice to impose "our way or the
highway." For example, they generally try to use their market muscle to
sabotage existing good standards (the browser wars come to mind) and impose
their own. So I join the ABM (anyone but MS) crowd here. Alas, they are now
so dominant, it is difficult on a practical (= good business decision) level
to do otherwise (a point made by others). Please do not dis the corporate
managers who must make such choices until you've been in their shoes.
Fortunately, I be not one of them.

Cheers,

Bert Gunter
Biometrics Research RY 32-305
Merck & Company
P.O. Box 2000
Rahway, NJ 07065-0900
Phone: (732) 594-7765   Fax: (732) 594-1565

"The business of the statistician is to catalyze the scientific learning
process."      -- George E.P. Box

messages.subject: Re: [S] RTF and S-Plus integration with other products
messages.subject_clean: [S] RTF and S-Plus integration with other products
messages.body_plain:
At 11/22/99 at 09:25 AM, Siem Heisterkamp wrote:

>> From Longhow Lam [lam at candiensten.nl] I heard that MathSoft has ideas to

integrate S-plus further with Word and Excel.  Personally I don't like that 
idea at all!  Please make S-PLus not more dependent on Microsoft. <<

I add my support to Dr. Heisterkamp's comments and those of other 
posters.  S-Plus should be independent of other software, yet able to 
exchange information with it.  Providing import and export filters is 
worthwhile, as is providing output in vendor-neutral and widely used 
formats, such as ASCII, RTF, and EPS.  Spending S-Plus development effort 
on integrating with a single vendor's products, especially products limited 
to a single platform, seems a waste.

The issue is not whether Microsoft and its products are "good" or "bad"; 
the issue is whether S-Plus development time is best spent on tight 
integration with any single vendor's current product line.

I'd rather see the development time and money spent on improving memory 
management, more testing, increased reliability, better help files and 
manuals, new procedures, and so on.  As to interoperability, it is better 
provided in the medium to long term by the use of vendor-neutral formats 
than by adopting other vendor's *current* formats and protocols; as well 
being limited to platform and product, such formats and protocols seem to 
be moving targets, prone to frequent change.

--
Michael Prager      <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516  USA

Standard Disclaimers: Opinions expressed here are personal
and are not otherwise represented.  Any use of tradenames
in the above does not constitute a NOAA endorsement.

[Smith, Stephen]  I would like to dip my oar into this contentious
sea as well.  I work in a Government Department in which computing
(Informatics as it is officially referred to) is more about control than
having the tools to get the job done.  We are officially a MS shop and at
first we had to spend a lot of energy explaining why packages like SPLUS
were necessary to Informatics managers who contended that Excel should be
enough.  As a LaTeX user I didn't even start explaining why I don't use
MSWord.  While it may be worthwhile fighting for principles here, I am also
a civil servant and like any good civil servant in a large bureaucracy I
need to pick my fights carefully.  Many of our official departmental forms
and reports are presently setup as Word templates and sometimes it is just
easier going with the flow rather than reinvent a small and rather minor
wheel.  In those cases I would prefer some form of integration of SPLUS
output with MS Word (getting rtf back would be a help).  Also some more work
on being able to import and edit graphics into word would also be helpful.
Currently (SP2000) trying to imbed and edit an SPLUS graphic more often than
not leads to page faults, black screens and hanging the system (which is one
a many reasons why I am a LaTeX user). 

        Stephen Smith

does anyone out there have some code written that will take in the
output from bicreg (by Raftery (and Volinsky)), and calculate the

and their ols coefficients - I simply need to calculate the variance for
each model separately, then combine the variance and the predictions
from each model to get an estimate of the mixed model variance...

If someone has this code or indeed other useful code to use in
conjunction with bicreg I'll gladly compile a set and re-distribute it
via s-news...

Thanks in advance

> It truly is impossible for anyone involved with administration to avoid
> using MS Office products, and I am surprised that Bill doesn't have to
> delve into Excel given that 90% of data that comes to me comes as an Excel

Yes, and this situation will only get worse unless we speak out in every
forum possible on behalf of open standards that allow multiple solutions
to interoperate smoothly.  What about (SYLK is it?) the spreadsheet
export language that supposedly allows sharing between different
spreadsheets?  I suppost that like many such standards, it may be
imperfect, in part due to customers not insisting on it being cleanly
implemented. The underlying point is that if the educated user does
not kick up his heels, nothing will ever improve.  We need to get our
organizations to realize what open standards are, to use them, and to
insist that vendors they deal with use them.  We need to kindly remind
our immediate colleagues that it is *rude* to send out a Word file
blindly assuming that the recipient can or should want to deal with it,
and to use non-proprietary subsitutes.  And yes, all this is a major
pain in the a**, but if we don't take it upon ourselves, how do we
*ever* climb out of Bill's little sandbox?  I for one refuse to use
any Microsoft product, and have never and will never pay them a cent.

Cheerio, Rick Rodgers

messages.subject: [S] Graph layout
messages.body_plain:
Working in Splus 4.0 on an NT.

I'm trying to produce a series of contour maps representing tree
abundance in two time periods.  The landscape in question has not
changed, just the distribution of the tree species.  I'd like to use the
same convex hull in both time periods in order to preserve the
geographical reference, but the approach is not very clear to me.

module(spatial)
attach(aspenglo)
aspenglo.spp <- as.spp(aspenglo)
aspen.chull <- aspenglo[chull(aspenglo),]
aspenglo.int <- interp(x, y, Percent)
win.graph()
par(mfcol=c(2,1))
plot(x, y, type="n", xlab="UTM EAST", ylab="UTM North", main="Aspen
Township Percentage GLO", cex=.35, boundary=T)
polygon(aspen.chull, den=0)
contour(aspenglo.int, nlevels=10, cex = .45, add = T)
detach("aspenglo")

attach(aspbirchimg)
aspbirchimg.spp <- as.spp(aspbirchimg)
aspbirch.chull <- aspbirchimg.spp[chull(aspbirchimg),]
aspbirch.int <- interp(x, y, percent)
plot(x, y, type="n", xlab="UTM EAST", ylab="UTM North", main="Aspen -
Birch - Conifers Township Percentage Imagery", cex=.35, boundary=T)
polygon(aspen.chull, den=0)
contour(aspbirch.int, nlevels=10, cex = .45, add = T)
detach("aspbirchimg")

This script produces the two maps, but the geometry for the second time
period is not correct.  I've simply substituted the chull for the first
time frame into the second call for the polygon.  I've also experimented
with the initial call for the chull in the third line of section of the
script with little success as well.

Any and all assistance is appreciated.

Thanks in advance
Steve Friedman

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 19 Nov 1999, Xiao Gang Su wrote:

> Bill's (Dunlap) Solution:
> =====================
> 
>        Count <- aggregate(rep(1, length(x)), list(x,y), sum)
>        names(Count)<-c("x","y","count")

Or for parsimony;

Count <- aggregate(list(count = rep(1, length(x))), list(x = x, y = y),
sum)

The first argument to aggregate.data.frame() is a data frame (or will be
converted to one) so using a named list for both the first and second
argument often works well.

messages.subject: [S] projection pursuit regression question
messages.body_plain:
Dear Readers,

I have a projection pursuit regression (PPR) question,
which relates to interpretation of Splus ppreg results.

In the original Friedman and Stuetzle (1981) paper,
the authors show how a simple interaction may be
re-coded in terms of two basis functions - i.e.,
 f(x,y) = xy = (1/4)(x+y)^2  - (1/4)(x-y)^2.
They then show how PPR as they implement it
uncovers essentially these two terms as basis functions.
The Splus manuals show the same example, and
show how "ppreg" does essentially the same thing.  

More generally, one can represent higher order polynomial
interaction terms in the same basis function way -
Diaconis and Shahshahani (1984) provide another example,
and I've worked out a few more myself.  

My question: has anyone extended Friedman and
Stuetzle's comparison to such higher order interaction terms,
or even compiled a list of what these terms would be?
This may be useful to know, to be able to interpret ppreg model fits
in the event one suspects that a data set contains such higher-order
interaction terms. 

Thank you for any replies - I'll summarize and repost them.

Regards,
Matt Kurbat

messages.subject: [S] S-PLUS, reports, and RTF
messages.body_plain:
At the risk of re-igniting a debate that seems to have died down, I'd like
to respond on behalf of MathSoft to the issues that were raised in the
discussion re reports and RTF.  

A number of people have commented recently on a change that MathSoft made
to the format of Report Files produced by versions of S-PLUS which run on
the Windows platform. The following discusses that change, in particular

        1.  What was changed,
        2.  The reason for the change, and
        3.  The implications of the change.

In S-PLUS 4.0 and S-PLUS 4.5, the default format for Report Files was RTF
(Rich Text Format) and the default file suffix was ".rtf". The advantage of
an RTF file is that it is not proprietary to any specific vendor. In other
words, it can be read by or imported into a number of word processing
programs on Windows, including WordPerfect and Word.

The disadvantage of using the RTF format is that it does not support
embedded ("live") links between S-PLUS Report Files and word processor
documents. A number of users complained about this and we listened. That
was the motivation for moving away from the RTF format. 

For the new format in S-PLUS 2000, we chose an off-the-shelf format called
"OLE Compound Document" format.  Only the new suffix, ".srp", is
proprietary.  The behavior of the new format is as follows:

1.  Any ".srp" file can be opened directly by WordPerfect (but not by
Word).

2. Any ".srp" can be inserted into a word processing program such as Word
or WordPerfect as an object (use the Insert/Object menu instead of the
File/Open menu in Word).  The resulting object can then be edited in the
word processor.  It will also be linked back to S-PLUS so that changes made
in the S-PLUS Report File will be reflected in the word processor document,
and changes made in the word processor document will be reflected back in
the S-PLUS Report File.  Embedded Report Files can include graphics which
have been copied and pasted from S-PLUS graphsheets.

3.  A Report File which contains only text (and not graphics) can be saved
as an RTF file using the "Save As" menu simply by changing the suffix from
".srp" to ".rtf".  It can then be opened by Word (and other word processing
programs) in the same manner as ".rtf" files produced by S-PLUS 4.0 or
S-PLUS 4.5.

Those users who have been asking us to revert to the old behavior should
use option 3 above. It is not necessary to wait for another release to get
the old behavior; you simply need to manually change the file suffix.  We
will look at making this a more explicit option in the next release.

Users interested in HTML output should refer to the help file for
"html.table".

A number of contributors to S-News have expressed the desire to avoid
Windows-specific solutions, even for versions of S-PLUS which run on
Windows.  For those users it should be noted that we do provide a "Text
only" format in the Report File "Save As" dialog. The resulting text-only
documents can be ported to Unix file systems using a standard utility such
as "dos2unix".  This feature is unchanged between S-PLUS 4.0, S-PLUS 4.5,
and S-PLUS 2000.

It is most unfortunate that we did not announce the above changes in our
Release Notes, nor did we document them in any other way.  For that we
sincerely apologize.  We will post a description of the changes on our web
site.

As always, I'm happy to receive any further comments by email.

# David

--

Dear S+ users,

I am working with S+ 4.5 under W95.

The 'axis' function allows to control labels and ticks along each axis
separately and is generally used after a 'plot(...axes=F...)' call.  The
orientation of the tick labels can be controlled by the 'las' parameter
(cf. help file).  However, this parameter has no effect if the 'at' and
'labels' parameters also receive explicit values (in fact it reacts

messages.body_plain:
Hello together,

I have set up a gam()-model and would like to test a set of variables
(each individually) in interaction with some factors in the model. To save
a lot of typing and comparing I would like to do this automatically.

I have tried to put the variable names in an array and then put them into
the model by using the 'index' of the array - but it did not work.

#### inital model
gamfit<-(EVENT ~ factor(SPELL)+  s(MONS1, df=8) + s(MONS2, df=8),               
na.action=na.gam.replace, family=binomial, data=data)   

### set of variables
array<-c("var1","var2","var3",...)

### put in interaction
gamfit.test<-(EVENT ~ factor(SPELL)+  s(MONS1, df=8) + s(MONS2, df=8)
+ s(MONS1, df=8):array[1],
na.action=na.gam.replace, family=binomial, data=data)

I tried also to put in paste("s(MONS1, df=8):",array[1], sep="") but it
did not work. 
the error I get is: Length of variable 5 is 1 != ROW NAMES

Obiously S+ does not 'connect' array[1] with the dataset, but just puts in
the first element of array, which it does not recognize as the variable of
the dataset.

The only thing I want to do is to put in another variable name by changing
the index of array[i].

any ideas?

thanks in advance!     Matthias

I am grateful to the comments about my problem with  printing PDF files from
Brian Ripley,  Bill Dunlap,  Dennis Murphy,  Charles Berry,  Simon Jackman,
and Jeff Simonoff.

The consensus seems to be:

(a) It also occurs on Linux. (Simon Jackman)
(b) The same file may print on one model of HP printer but not on another
(both in postscript mode). (Jeff Simonoff)
(c) The bug is in Adobe Acrobat Reader  (Jeff Simonoff, Bill Dunlap, Brian
Ripley)
(d) The problem occurs with some versions of  Acrobat Reader and not with
others.
(e) MathSoft is aware of the problem but has no fix for it.
(f) For Windows, one workaround is to use wmf2eps  as Export Graph produces
such poor eps files(Brian Ripley).

There are shareware and free programmes available which convert wmf to png
(which can be included in TeX files and then converted into pdf files). I

A few weeks ago Prof Ripley posted 

   in which no one can see anything unless it is pointed out to them (and
then
   only a very few can) yet I can get significance levels less than 10^{-4}
   from a statistical test of there being something there (and there is).

in response to

.. in applied statistics if you cannot see an effect with graphics you will
never see it with statistics

but this seems to implicitly imply that "the best way or at least a good
way" to graph it has been determined. 

Now if one loosely defines an important effect as being a large ratio of the
effect to the variation/uncertainty of it  
(for some clever definition of effect) then the claim would become one David
Andrews has made many times 
"if we are clever enough, the significance of an effect can almost always be
determined by a simple t-test"

(On the other hand, the locating of an effect and its recognition when
poorly defined (not ideally graphed) is quite 
a different matter and Prof Ripley's comment is very interesting in that
regard)

Hope this is of some interest and not too late

Keith O'Rourke
Statistician, Department of Surgery and Clinical Epidemiology Unit
University of Ottawa/ Ottawa Hospital

previous post

Sure, but not quite always. One of my favourite demos at the moment is a
functional MRI dataset of 2 million points (100 sets of images in sequence)
in which no one can see anything unless it is pointed out to them (and then
only a very few can) yet I can get significance levels less than 10^{-4}
from a statistical test of there being something there (and there is).  It
is the ability to do problems that are beyond the human visual system that
are `modern' (and as you pointed out, depend on hardware developments).  
As I understand it `data visualization' is a _much_ larger research subject
than Cleveland's (1993) book (and was in 1993). Things like projection
pursult, multidimensional scaling, correspondence analysis, biplots, ...
are important data visualization tools (and dare I say much more important
than Trellis(TM) graphics), and there is a computer science literature,
even on `caves' and virtual reality immersion, ....

Brian Ripley

--

This raises a point that may be of interest to the general user of
visualization approaches (not just limited to the Trellis approach, but
including other approaches mentioned by Prof. Ripley). What if it's the
other way around? What if one can clearly see an effect through graphics,
but it is not obvious to the general user how to test that effect with
statistics (eg. in multivariate studies where one's data is far from
'ideal')? Is it still legitimate to publish  the finding relying entirely on
visualization? My feeling is that this is the scenario in which one is most
likely to run into trouble with referees...

PS. Although most of this thread has been 'public', I will summarize asap.

messages.subject: Re: [S] the function "approx" with "apply"
messages.body_plain:
> apply(RawData, 1, approx, x = RawData[, 1:8], 
>       y = RawData[, 9:16], xout = Terms, 
>       method = "linear", rule = 3) 

> where RawData is a matrix with size of 270 by 16 and xout is a
> vector with size of 7.  The statement produces identical 270
> $y's which all should be distinct.  Thank you for your help.

I can only guess at what you wanted to do but I presume you meant
to use

apply(RawData, 1, function(x)
               approx(x = x[1:8], y = x[9:16], xout = Terms, 
               rule = 3))

In any case your call produced unexpected results only because
your model for the way apply() works is incorrect.  When you use

    apply(M, 1, fun,   .....)

you should think of the function `fun' being handed one row of M
at a time as its first argument.  The function then only has to
say what should be done with that row.  

If I have correctly guessed what you meant to do above,
additional arguments are not needed in this case as they can be
built into the anonymous function that you use as the third
argument to apply().

It would be convenient if there were some way in S-PLUS to
traverse several parallel structures at once (as your attempt
above seems to imply) but this is not presently available.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: C/C++ question
messages.body_plain:
By (some) popular demand, I post the original question and the summary
of the responses that I have received. Thanks much to everyone that has
replied!

Original question:

> Dear all,
>
> I apologize if this is the wrong outlet for my question but I could
not
> think of a better newsgroup. I was wondering whether somebody had any
> experience with MatClass
> (a matrix class for C++) available at
ftp://ftp.mcc.ac.uk/pub/matclass/.
> More generally, I also would be grateful for pointers to freeware
C/C++
> code for linear regression and related topics. Currently, I am using
the
> SVD based routines from Numerical Recipes but I was hoping to find
> something (almost) as accurate but significantly faster.

Responses:

Robert Davies wrote:

Look at my site http://webnz.com/robert for my C++ matrix class library
and also for my list of other C++ sites.

The QR decomposition is probably good enough for you and is faster than
SVD. If you are doing analysis of variance type analyses then old
fashioned
normal equations (after removing the means) may be good enough and may
be
a lot faster. The example in my matrix library illustrates these methods

in a "toy" example but you could apply them to a real problem.

Nick Ellis wrote:

Here are two matrix libraries; I think the first has SVD. I'm not so
sure
about the second (Blitz++), but according to the web pages it seems very

comprehensive. You can't run Blitz++ with Visual C++ though. Would you
please let me know if you have any success with these, as I am beginning
to
explore matrix C++ libraries myself.

http://nz.com/webnz/robert/nzc_nm09.html

http://oonumerics.org/blitz/manual/Frames.html

Nick Ellis
CSIRO Marine Research   mailto:Nick.Ellis at marine.csiro.au
PO Box 120                      ph    +61 (07) 3826 7260
Cleveland QLD 4163      fax   +61 (07) 3826 7222
Australia                       http://www.marine.csiro.au

Tony Rossini wrote:

I like Meschach (available from netlib).  It's a pretty complete,
nicely written and better yet, documented, C matrix/numerical linear
algebra library.

best,
-tony

I have not had the time yet to try any of the C++ matrix classes (to
speed up my regressions I am using LU and QR decompositions from
Numerical Recipes instead of SVD for the moment) but if/when I do so, I
will post my findings.

Thanks again,
Michael

messages.subject: [S] Testing interactions in anova
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I have a problem in understanding  two features connected with the anova in
S-plus (4.5).
1) when specifying a model with an interaction term (say A:C) but with one of
the first order terms missing I get the following result:

****
aov(formula = y ~ A + B + A:C, data = Exlez3.2.df)

Estimated effects are balanced

          Df Sum of Sq Mean Sq F Value   Pr(F)
        A  1      1871    1871      211.7     0.00000
        B  1         68        68          7.7     0.01805
    A:C  2        281      140        15.9     0.00057
Residuals 11        97       9

Estimated Coefficients:
 (Intercept)     A      B   A1C   A2C
       70.81 10.81 -2.062 -4.25 4.125
*****
The results for the full model are the following:

****
aov(formula = y ~ A * B * C, data = Exlez3.2.df)

         Df Sum of Sq Mean Sq F Value  Pr(F)
        A      1      1871    1871   165.4  0.0000
        B      1        68      68        6.0    0.0398
        C      1         0       0          0.0    0.9426
      A:B    1         0       0          0.0    0.9426
      A:C    1       281     281      24.8    0.0011
      B:C    1         5       5           0.4    0.5224
    A:B:C   1         2       2          0.1    0.7198
Residuals  8        90      11
****

In Modern Applied Statistics with S-plus(3rd ed, page 184) I read that it is
"statistically meaningless or futile" to fit an interaction term without all
the corresponding marginal terms . Can somebody explain me the statistical
sense of pooling together the SS of A:C and C?
Doesn't it bias the F value and lower the power of the test?  (note that the
pvalue for A:C in the reduced model is lower than that in the full model only
because of the removal of other  terms).

I don't want to start a polemic about the effect heridariety principle ;) I am
just unhappy about the default behaviour of S-Plus. (I  know that I can avoid
this behaviour adding a -C term).

2) when calling qqnorm.aov the points plotted are more than the effects
included in the model. What are these points and how are they calculated? I
couldn't find any reference to them. By the way, does anybody know why the
options FULL=F was removed from the qqnorm command?

I have just subscribed to this list so I am not sure if my questions have
already been answered (I did search the archive).

thanks in advance, Giovanni Merola

messages.subject: Re: [S] Testing interactions in anova
messages.body_plain:
Giovanni Merola wrote

> In Modern Applied Statistics with S-plus(3rd ed, page 184) I read
> that it is "statistically meaningless or futile" to fit an
> interaction term without all the corresponding marginal terms . Can
> somebody explain me the statistical sense of pooling together the SS
> of A:C and C?

First of all you have to say what you mean by A:C when C and/or A are
not present.  One does this by placing constraints on the parameters
which specify the model which includes main effects.  It is the only
way one can do it.  One then has to ask: "Why this particular form
of constraints?"

Where there are several factors and/or variables, there are a huge
number of models that one might fit.  One reduces the selection task
to managable proportions by imposing a hierarchy on the terms that are
examined: main effects, first order interactions, second order, ...
Similarly with orthogonal polynomials: linear, then quadratic, then
cubic.  We do not usually try whether we can drop the linear and
quadratic components when the cubic component is added!  When fitting
splines we impose a comparable hierarchy on the basis terms that we
use.

Also, it seems that the passion for fitting second order interactions
with `main effects' constrained to be the same for all levels of the
factor rarely extends to fitting third order interactions while
placing comparable constraints on one or both of main effects and
first order interactions.  Why not?  Why for that matter not try all
manner of other constraints on main effects or on interactions or ...

Why do we work within these hierarchies?  This structured approach to
model fitting limits the number of models that we need to contemplate.
We start with the simplest possible model (additive effects) and add
only as much additional complication as we can justify.  Moreover we
do this in a structured manner.

Where there are many factors and variables, we may have to impose
even stronger structure on the hierachy of models that we contemplate
in order to get anywhere.  (e. g. test all first order interactions
in a single fell swoop).

> Doesn't it bias the F value and lower the power of the test?  (note
> that the pvalue for A:C in the reduced model is lower than that in
> the full model only because of the removal of other terms).

But what are you testing?  Why did you place this particular form of
constraint on the paremeters?  I'd say that the F value is biased by
the constraints that are imposed.

> I don't want to start a polemic about the effect heridariety
> principle ;) I am just unhappy about the default behaviour of
> S-Plus. (I know that I can avoid this behaviour adding a -C term).

Well, maybe that is what you have.  It is also part of the way the
world is that these issues are connected.

> 2) when calling qqnorm.aov the points plotted are more than the effects
> included in the model. What are these points and how are they calculated? I
> couldn't find any reference to them. By the way, does anybody know why the
> options FULL=F was removed from the qqnorm command?

> I have just subscribed to this list so I am not sure if my questions have
> already been answered (I did search the archive).

The issue does come up regularly, in various guises.  I thought I'd try
a rather different tack from the answers that have been given earlier.

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY: data visualization references
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who responded to my question regarding data visualization and
the problems associated with convincing referees that it is a valid
approach. I am clearly not the only one experiencing such problems, and I
received many useful suggestions and references, I list below the ones that
have not already been posted to the list.

Thanks again,
Willem

On Fri, 19 Nov 1999, I asked:

> 
> Fellow S-users,
> 
> Please excuse me for bothering you with a problem only tangentially
related
> to S-plus. I'm submitting a review article based on a multivariate study
> which benefited greatly from the various visualization methods described
by
> Cleveland (1993; and incorporated in the Trellis library) for both my
> univariate and multivariate analyses. I'm having trouble with one referee
> who writes that a "major problem is that the paper uses a "visualization"
> technique to analyze the data". I have, of course, referred to Cleveland's
> book, but the referee is not satisfied. I have only very little space to
> work with, can any one point me to an independent reference for the
current
> status of visualization in modern data analysis and statistics? Any
> suggestions for a brief definition of "data visualization"?

No, not really: it is a very large subject and Cleveland's work is a tiny
(and somewhat isolated) corner that is (deliberately or otherwise)
neglected outside the S community. (I think the neglect is mutual.)

-- 
Brian D. Ripley,                  ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk
Professor of Applied Statistics,  http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/
University of Oxford,             Tel:  +44 1865 272861 (self)
1 South Parks Road,                     +44 1865 272860 (secr)
Oxford OX1 3TG, UK                Fax:  +44 1865 272595

Hello,

i had similar problems. The referees are just simply not ready yet to accept
these really
top class graphics from Cleveland.

Tufte:

The Visual Display of Quantitative Information 
by Edward R. Tufte
Hardcover Reprint edition (February 1992) 
Graphics Press; ISBN: 096139210X ; Dimensions (in inches): 0.87 x 10.92 x
9.01 

Wilkinson:

The Grammar of Graphics (Statistics and Computing) 
by Leland Wilkinson 
Hardcover - 408 pages (August 1999) 
Springer Verlag; ISBN: 0387987746 ; Dimensions (in inches): 1.06 x 9.24 x
6.30 

Greetings

Marcel
Marcel.Baumgartner at rdls.nestle.com

Hi Willem,

Just met the same problem (not yet solved...). You can cite the paper:
Becker, R.A., Cleveland, W.S. and Shyu, M.-J., 1996. The visual design
and control of trellis display. Journal of Computational and Graphical
Statistics, 5 (2): 123-155.

which is available at:
http://www.research.att.com/~rab/trellis/index.html

There is also a small document called "Trellis Display: Questions and
Answers" available at
http://www.research.att.com/areas/stat/doc/index.html

which might give you some ideas for "referee-oriented" explanations...

I would be very interested to get other private replies that would come
to you.

Best regards,

Renaud

-- 
Dr Renaud Lancelot, vétérinaire

The main thing to remember is that not every referee can be be satisfied on 
every point.  Sometimes there are honest disagreements, and not 
infrequently referees are just plain wrong!  You may need to tell the 
editor you disagree with the referee, and why.

That said,  you might find the following books useful, either as direct 
citations or as sources of further citations:

Tukey, J. W.  1977.  Exploratory data analysis.  Addison-Wesley, Reading 
Massachusetts.  499 pp.

Tufte, E. R.  1983.  The visual display of quantitative 
information.  Graphics Press, Cheshire, Connecticut.  197 pp.

Tufte, E. R.  1990.  Envisioning information.  Graphics Press, Cheshire, 
Connecticut.  126 pp.

Spence, I., and S. Lewandowsky.  1990.  Graphical perception.  Chapter 2 in 
Modern methods of data analysis, J. Fox and J. S. Long, eds.  Sage 
Publications, Newbury Park, California.  446 pp.

Further references can probably be obtained from the bibliographies of the 
reports available at

http://netlib.bell-labs.com/cm/ms/departments/sia/doc/index.html#vis

and

http://netlib.bell-labs.com/cm/ms/departments/sia/project/trellis/index.html

I hope this helps.

--
Michael Prager                     <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516

Hoaglin, Mosteller, & Tukey  have a
series of books with Wiley in which they often stress the use of simply
looking at your data, or at summaries of results.  One is

H, M & T, _Fundamentals of Exploratory Analysis of Variance_, in which
they
talk about ways to look at effects and residuals.  

Also H, M & T, _Exploring Data Tables, Trends, and Shapes_.

They'll probably have even more references.

Good luck,

Matt Wiener

Willem,
Have you referenced Venables & Riple's book, "Modern Applied Statistics with
S-Plus"?
This book emphasizes the use of visualization for data analysis and
visualizing statistical results (see Chapter 1, Introduction). This should
satisfy the referee.
Eric

Eric Grunsky, Ph.D., P.Geol.
Associate Editor, Computers & Geosciences (http://www.iamg.org)
Assistant Editor,  Natural Resources Research
Editorial Board, Journal of Geochemical Exploration (http://www.aeg.org)

Willem,

The classic reference to data visualization is

Tufte, E.R.  1983. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information.  Chesire,
CT: Graphics Press.

Additional references are
Cleveland W.S. 1994.  The Elements of Graphing Data (2nd ed.)  Summit, NJ:
Hobart Press.

Wainer, H.  1997.  Visual Revelations:  Graphical Tales of Fate and
Deception
from Napolean Bonaparte to Ross Perot. New York:  Copernicus.

See also the references in Wainer.

For an important case study of visualization see Cleveland's 1993, review of
the Barley data set in Chap 6 of Visualizing Data.  In this case, the visual
approach revealed an error in the data that no formal analyses since 1934
had
never noticed.

Joe

presentation of information: 
 
The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. 1983 
Envisioning Information. 1990 
Visual Explanations. 1997 

http://public.logica.com/~stepneys/bib/nf/tufte.htm
