messages.body_plain:

In GLM, if Yi are the observations and L the link function, L(E(Yi)) is
supposed to be a linear combination
 of the covariates.  The unknown coefficients of this combination can be
estimated using the 'glm' function.  If some or all 
of the factors are random, one could be interested in the variances
associated to them in place of the individual coefficients
 values.  The function 'varcomp' do that for linear models.  What can we

messages.subject: [S] Some agony -- no ecstasy
messages.body_plain:
S-Plus Folks:

I recently spent longer than I wish to publicly acknowledge tracking down
the following S-Plus "bad" behavior. Well, not really -- more my ignorance
of normal S-Plus behavior. Now while Brian (Ripley) may point out that I
should have known -- and I agree, I should have -- the fact is that I
didn't, and it certainly wasn't something that sticks in my mind as widely
publicized. So to save other innocents(?) the suffering, I will "broadcast"
the info in this forum. Hope it's useful. 

Suppose I've got a bunch of data ("large data set" seems a characterization
fraught with peril these days) of the following form:

> z <- matrix(rnorm(100000), nc = 2)
> fct <- sample(1:100, 50000, repl = T)

I want to get, say, the means of the groups defined by fct for each column.
tapply() seems like a simple way to do it (other ideas welcome):

> dos.time(tapply(1:50000, fct, function(x, y)
c(mean(y[x, 1]), mean(y[x, 2])), z))

[1] 0.2803

Fair enough. Suppose now I make z a data.frame. How long does it take now?

> z <- as.data.frame(z)
> dos.time(tapply(1:50000, fct, function(x, y)
c(mean(y[x, 1]), mean(y[x, 2])), z))

[1] 3.391

Wow! More than 10 times as long! Is this due to some kind of data.frame
overhead?

> z <- as.matrix(z)
> dos.time(tapply(1:50000, fct, function(x, y)
c(mean(y[x, 1]), mean(y[x, 2])), z))

[1] 3.14

Nope, not really. Why then? Well, here's the culprit:

> dimnames(z) <- NULL
> dos.time(tapply(1:50000, fct, function(x, y)
c(mean(y[x, 1]), mean(y[x, 2])), z))

[1] 0.2793

It's those darn row.names that got tacked on by the data.frame() command and
stay around unless explicitly excised. 

Moral of the tale: Beware the baggage of row names -- and watch out that
they don't get tacked on for you when you're not looking. Hope this saves
others my travail.

Cheers to all,

Bert Gunter
Biometrics Research RY 32-305
Merck & Company
PO Box 2000
Rahway, NJ 07065-0900
Phone: (732)594-7765  Fax:594-1565

messages.subject: [S] Summary: memory constraints using predict()
messages.body_plain:
Several people emailed me expressing their surprise that generating kriged 
predictions over a grid of about 15000 points should take over 2 days, given my 
hardware configuration (original message below). Several people suggested that 
I increase my RAM-to-Swap ratio...I only wish I could! However, Prof. Ripley 
suggested succinctly the most straightforward solution: 

> Do it in slices of a few hundred points at a time. 

Of course! Sometimes the solutions are so simple, they make you feel like an 
idiot when someone else has to point them out :o)

So I wrote a little script to generate predictions over about 500 points at a 
time...but it still took about 15 minutes to complete 1 run of 500! To me this 
seems far too long for a paultry 500 points using predict(). When the second 
line of the script ran I noticed that at the bottom of the script window 
numerous warning messages were scrolling by. As it turns out the predictions do 
appear to be "correct", so I'm not sure why the warnings were generated 
(another investigation required). Anyway, the point is that after turning the 
warning message off > options(warn=-1) < the entire script took about 30 
seconds to complete. I even ran the original predict() function again and this 
time it took about 20 seconds to complete for all 14746 points!

Take home message: Functions that generate repeated warning messages eat up a 
tremendous amount of processing time.

Partial solution (fixing the function notwithstanding):

Check to see if the function is producing warning messages by either running 
the function in a script window or have Splus display warnings immediately 
>options(warn=0)<, rather than once the function has completed (which is the 
default). If numerous warnings are being produced but the function output is 
correct, you can eliminate the warnings: >options(warn=-1). 

However, I would recommend that you _not_ leave this setting as the default 
and, of course, that you try to find the actual source of the warnings and fix 
it!

Thanks to Prof. Ripley for the workable solution and to others who shared their 
own experiences and frustrations.

Cheers,

Ian Jonsen

>I'm running Splus 2000 with the SpatialStats module under Win95, I have a 450 
>MHZ PIII with 128 Mb Ram and ~ 2Gb >swap space.

>I'm trying to generate kriging predictions over an evenly spaced grid of 14746 
>points (called elev.pgrid20) using predict()

>>predict(elev.krig,newdata=elev.pgrid20)

>The function has been running for almost 2 days and still hasn't completed! 
>Amazingly the system hasn't crashed, the hard >drive is still spooling 
>(writing to the swap file continuously it would seem). Can anyone tell me if 
>there is some way to >improve the efficiency here?? 

_______________________________________

messages.subject: Re: [S] SUMMARY: data visualization references
messages.body_plain:
Perhaps it would be helpful to have one other perspective, that of a referee.
My experience as an author of manuscripts has run the gamut so I can't
generalize about referees. However, I have been the referee of editors' choice
for several journals where authors have appealed or resubmitted over
statistical issues. I have played a similar role for granting agencies.

It is amazing the number of manuscripts where there is no discernible reason
for the form of statistical analysis other than a reference to the package
documentation, hence, referees conclude such authors have little sense of what
is needed. For grants I often suggest weak proposals be resubmitted after
consultation with a statistician. For papers I look for contact with the
relevant statistical and disciplinary literature which demonstrates what is
appropriate for the specific content of the paper. Establish that the specific
problem is best addressed with the procedure. Depending on the circumstances it
may or may not be necessary to even identify S+ or SAS or xlispstat as the
means of carrying out the procedure. If an author can show why a particular
visualization is appropriate for the particular data I would not demand what
program he used to create the visual. It should be clear to the reader (or
referee) that the visual illuminates the data and is not present simply because
the author likes visuals or his software generates visuals.
